header.html: Domain IV, Governing AI deployment and use (21 to 25 questions)
IV.C, Govern the system while it is deployed and in use (blueprint 9–11 questions)

IV.C.1 Apply policies, practices and ethics when deploying and using the system; IV.C.2 Monitor continuously and schedule maintenance, updates and retraining in use; IV.C.3 Run periodic checks of performance, reliability and safety in use; IV.C.4 Keep records of incidents, issues, risks and the plan for monitoring after release; IV.C.5 Forecast and reduce secondary or unintended uses and downstream harm; IV.C.6 Set up external communication plans; IV.C.7 Put in place the policy and controls to deactivate or localize a system
EU AI Act (Articles 4, 5, 12, 14, 25, 26, 50, 72, 73), GDPR (Article 33), NIST AI RMF (GOVERN, MEASURE 3, MANAGE 2 and 4), NIST AI 600-1, New York City Local Law 144
Module 13 of the course. Read after Module 12.

[Beyond the BoK] = needed to answer questions but not stated in the Body of Knowledge text. [Dates] = a date to know. [Verify live] = the law was still moving when written; the slide shows an "as of" date.
Acronyms in this note. GDPR: General Data Protection Regulation

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Apply policies, practices and ethics to a system in use: user training, issue management, data governance and risk management
  • Run monitoring, and a schedule of maintenance, updates and retraining, from the deployer's side
  • Carry out periodic checks of performance, reliability and safety
  • Keep records of incidents, issues and risks, and of monitoring plans
  • Forecast and reduce secondary and unintended uses and the harm they do downstream
  • Set up external communication plans
  • Put in place the policy and controls to switch a system off or limit it by region

2IV.C.1: Apply policies, practices and ethics when deploying and using the system

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Apply, so the depth is Apply. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Running case

Oversight, a Misused Assistant and a Switched-Off Feature

  • Lucia Moreno's recruiters review the hiring tool's ranking before any decision; the oversight must be real, not a rubber stamp
  • A recruiter uses the customer assistant to rank résumés, a use it was never approved for
  • Samira Haddad asks for an external communication plan for the assistant and the hiring tool
  • The emotion-analysis feature is switched off in the EU and limited by region elsewhere
  • Your task: govern the two systems while they are in use

Deployment Governance: Policies, Procedures and Roles

  • Putting a system into use means applying the organization's policies (module 3), not writing new ones
  • Owner: one named business owner is accountable for the system in use
  • Procedures: a deployment checklist, change control and an escalation path
  • Four practices run through use: user training, issue management, data governance and risk management
  • Ethics: the values and red lines in the policy decide what the system may be used for
  • Helios: Lucia Moreno owns the hiring tool; Anika Berg owns the assistant

Exam tip

Policies exist before deployment; deployment governance applies them to the system in use.

Data Governance and Risk Management in Use

  • Input data: the deployer controls what goes in; for a high-risk system it must ensure input data are relevant and sufficiently representative (Article 26)
  • Rules for users: what may be entered (no confidential or special-category data unless approved) and where outputs may go
  • Knowledge sources: owners, review dates and versions for the documents the system draws on (module 11)
  • Privacy: retention limits, access control and a lawful basis (module 4)
  • Risk management: the risk register is updated from monitoring, feedback and incidents, not left at its launch version
  • Helios: the support documents get owners and review dates after the wrong refund answer
Exam tip

In use, data governance covers the inputs and sources the deployer controls, and the risk register stays alive.

Issue Management: From Report to Fix

  • An issue is a problem found in use: a wrong output, a complaint, a workaround or a gap in a document
  • Channel: an easy way for users and affected people to report, with an owner who reads it
  • Flow: log, triage by severity, assign, fix, verify and close
  • Link to incidents: an issue that causes or could cause harm moves to the incident process (module 10)
  • Patterns: repeated issues point to a systemic cause and go to the committee
  • NIST GOVERN 5.1: policies collect and integrate feedback from people outside the team
Exam tip

An issue log without owners and dates is only a list.

User Training and Acceptable Use

  • Training by role: operators, reviewers, support staff and managers each need a different depth (module 2)
  • AI literacy: Article 4 asks deployers to take measures to support the development of AI literacy of staff and others who use the system
  • Oversight competence: people given oversight of a high-risk system need competence, training and authority (Article 26)
  • Acceptable-use rules: what the tool is for, what it is not for, what data may go in, and how to report problems
  • Refresh the training after major changes, incidents and new rules
  • Helios: recruiters learn to read the ranking, when to disagree and why not to paste résumés into the assistant
Exam tip

Training is a control: people given oversight must be able to understand, question and override.

Meaningful Human Oversight and Transparency to Users Beyond the BoK

  • Meaningful oversight means the person can understand the system, interpret its output, and decide not to use, override or reverse it (Article 14)
  • Automation bias: the habit of trusting the output too much; training, time and incentives must make disagreement normal
  • Stop control: a way to intervene or stop the system
  • Transparency to users: tell people they are interacting with AI, tell those exposed to emotion recognition (Article 50), and tell affected people that a high-risk system supports decisions about them (Article 26)
  • Not a rubber stamp: measure override rates and review samples
  • Helios: the recruiters see the reasons for a ranking and may overrule it
Exam tip

Oversight is meaningful only if the person can understand, disagree and act on the disagreement.

3IV.C.2: Monitor continuously and schedule maintenance, updates and retraining in use

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Conduct, so the depth is Apply. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

What the Deployer Monitors

  • The deployer watches the system in its own setting, with its own users and data
  • Outputs and accuracy against the thresholds from the impact assessment
  • Inputs and drift: shifts in who and what the system sees (module 10)
  • Fairness of outcomes for your own groups, and feedback and overrides
  • Security and misuse: unusual queries, abuse and data leakage
  • Provider changes: new versions, notices and incidents at the vendor

Exam tip

The deployer monitors the system in its own setting; the provider's monitoring cannot see that.

Maintenance, Updates and Retraining in Use

  • Two sources of change: the provider's and your own
  • Provider changes: new versions, patches and withdrawals; use the contract's notice and retest terms (module 12)
  • Your changes: prompts, settings, thresholds, knowledge sources and any retraining or fine-tuning
  • Schedule: regular reviews, patch windows and document refreshes, plus triggered changes after drift or incidents
  • Change control: test, approve, release in stages, monitor and roll back if needed (module 10)
  • Record the version, settings and approver of every change

Exam tip

Every change, whoever makes it, goes through the same test, approve, release and monitor routine.

Feedback and Escalation to the Provider

  • Tell the provider: a deployer of a high-risk system must monitor operation and inform the provider, suspend use where there is a risk, and report any serious incident (Article 26)
  • Use the contract: incident notice, support channels and service reviews (module 12)
  • Share evidence: logs, examples and test results, with privacy protected
  • Escalate inside: unresolved issues go to the business owner, then the committee
  • Track the answers: the provider's fixes and dates go in the issue log
  • NIST: communicate incidents and errors to relevant AI actors, including affected communities (MANAGE 4.3)
Exam tip

A deployer who sees a problem and keeps quiet loses both the fix and the chance to show diligence.

4IV.C.3: Run periodic checks of performance, reliability and safety in use

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Conduct, so the depth is Apply. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Periodic Checks: Schedule and Scope

  • Periodic checks step back from continuous monitoring to ask whether the system is still performing, reliable and safe in use
  • Set the schedule by risk, and also run checks after major changes
  • The table shows five checks: metrics, samples, assessment refresh, security tests and vendor review
  • Owners run each check and report to the committee
  • Evidence: keep the results, even when nothing is found
  • Helios: hiring-tool metrics each quarter; assistant samples each month

Exam tip

Continuous monitoring watches; periodic checks test.

Audits and Reviews in Use

  • Internal audit (the third line, module 2) checks that the system in use follows policy and that controls work
  • Vendor audit rights (module 12): use them, or ask for independent reports
  • Independent bias audits: some laws require them, such as New York City's rule for hiring tools, with a public summary
  • Scope: policy compliance, training records, logs, issue and incident handling, and monitoring evidence
  • Findings get owners and due dates, and follow-up checks closure
  • Helios: internal audit reviews hiring-tool oversight; an independent bias audit is arranged for New York City
Exam tip

An audit looks backward at evidence; it does not replace monitoring.

Red Teaming and Security Testing of Your Own Setup

  • The deployer's setup has its own weak points: system prompts, knowledge sources, connections and user habits
  • Red team your configuration: try misuse, injection through documents, data extraction and out-of-scope requests (module 10)
  • Threat model new connections and features before they ship
  • Security tests: access control, logging, data leakage and third-party components
  • Reliability checks: failure handling, fallbacks to a person and recovery
  • Retest after every significant change
Exam tip

A provider's testing does not cover your configuration, so test it yourself.

Acting on Findings: Continue, Limit or Suspend

  • Every check ends in a decision: continue, continue with fixes, limit or suspend
  • Severity decides: harm to people, legal duty and scale
  • Findings become actions with owners, dates and retests
  • Report results and trends to the business owner and the committee
  • Update the risk register, the impact assessment and the training
  • Suspending use (where there is a risk) and informing the provider (for a risk or a serious incident) are required (Article 26)
Exam tip

A check that never changes anything is not working.

5IV.C.4: Keep records of incidents, issues, risks and the plan for monitoring after release

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Document, so the depth is Apply. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Three Registers: Incidents, Issues and Risks in Use

  • Incident register: every incident and near miss, with severity, cause, actions and closure
  • Issue log: problems found in use, with owner, due date and evidence of closure
  • Risk register: risks, likelihood, severity, controls, owners and status
  • Link them: an incident updates the risks, and repeated issues point to a risk
  • Deployer view: include provider incidents that affect you, and complaints from affected people
  • Review the registers at each committee meeting: trends matter
Exam tip

Records are evidence: what is not written down cannot be shown.

Logs and Retention

  • Automatic logs let you trace what the system did; providers design logging in (Article 12), and deployers keep the logs under their control for at least six months (Article 26)
  • What to log: inputs, outputs, versions, user actions, overrides and alerts
  • Protect them: access controls and limits, since logs may hold personal data (module 4)
  • Retention balance: long enough for investigations and duties, and no longer than privacy rules allow for personal data
  • Use them for incident investigation, audits and monitoring
  • NIST: track, respond to and document incidents and errors (MANAGE 4.3)
Exam tip

Logs serve oversight, but they can also be personal data: keep what you need and protect it.

Monitoring Plans: The Provider's Plan and the Deployer's Part

  • The provider runs a post-market monitoring system and plan for the product (Article 72), collecting and analyzing performance data over its lifetime
  • The deployer has its own part: it monitors operation and feeds information back to the provider (Article 26)
  • Document your own monitoring plan: what is watched, by whom, thresholds, alerts, reviews and escalation (module 10)
  • Align the two plans: who sends what to whom, how often and in which format
  • Update the plan when the system, the use or the risks change
  • Helios: Lucia Moreno's team keeps the hiring-tool plan and sends feedback to Veridex
Exam tip

The provider's plan covers the product; the deployer's plan covers the use.

Who Reports What to Whom

  • Deployer to provider: inform the provider, suspend use where there is a risk, and report any serious incident (Article 26)
  • Provider to authority: the provider reports serious incidents (Article 73), with the clocks from module 10
  • Personal data breach: the controller notifies the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours (GDPR Article 33)
  • Contracts and sector rules may add shorter notices
  • Affected people are informed as the rules and the communication plan require
  • Record who was told, when and what

Exam tip

One event can start several clocks: the shortest applicable one governs.

6IV.C.5: Forecast and reduce secondary or unintended uses and downstream harm

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Forecast, so the depth is Apply. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Secondary and Unintended Uses

  • A system approved for one purpose gets used for others
  • Secondary use: a new purpose beyond the approved one
  • Unintended use: a use the builders did not foresee, often by well-meaning staff
  • Misuse: deliberate harmful use
  • Downstream harm: harm to people or systems that receive or rely on the output
  • NIST warns about off-label use of AI built for other purposes

Exam tip

Most unintended use is not malicious: it is convenient.

Forecasting Misuse and Downstream Harm

  • Ask early: who else could use this system, for what, and what happens next?
  • Four lenses: the busy user who takes shortcuts, the curious user who tries everything, the bad actor, and the downstream receiver who relies on the output
  • Methods: use-case workshops, pre-mortems, red teaming and scenario analysis
  • Evidence: query logs, feedback and shadow-use surveys show how the system is really used
  • Link to the impact assessment: add the forecast uses and their harms
  • Rate each by likelihood and severity, and plan controls (module 8)

Exam tip

Forecast by asking who else, for what, and what happens next.

Reducing the Risk: Scope, Access, Monitoring and Training

  • State the scope: intended and out-of-scope uses, in the system and in the instructions to users
  • Control access: least privilege; only the people and features that need it
  • Technical limits: system prompt limits, filters, blocked actions and rate limits
  • Monitor: alerts for out-of-scope queries, and review of logs and shadow use
  • People: training, user agreements and clear consequences
  • A change of purpose needs a new assessment; a deployer that changes the intended purpose so that a system becomes high-risk is treated as its provider (Article 25(1))

Exam tip

Say what the system is for and not for, then back it with access limits and monitoring.

When Harm Travels Downstream

  • Downstream harm happens after the output leaves your system: a customer repeats a wrong answer, a partner reuses data, a decision rests on a draft
  • Mark outputs: say they are AI-generated, with limits and the need to check
  • Contract terms: license limits for partners and resellers, and no use for prohibited purposes
  • Track onward use where you can: APIs, exports and shared datasets
  • Value-chain risk: NIST lists value chain and component integration among the twelve generative AI risks
  • Fix and notify when downstream harm is found: corrections, notices and withdrawal of outputs
Exam tip

Responsibility does not stop at the output: plan for what others do with it.

7IV.C.6: Set up external communication plans

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Establish, so the depth is Apply. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Who Needs to Hear What

  • An external communication plan says who is told what, when, by whom and through which channel
  • Audiences: users and customers, affected people, regulators, providers and partners, staff, and the public and media
  • Each audience needs different content, in plain language
  • Cover routine communication (notices) and event-driven communication (incidents, changes, shutdowns)
  • Align it with legal duties and with the contract
  • Approve content with legal, privacy, communications and the business owner

Exam tip

Plan the audiences first, then the messages.

Notices, Explanations and Incident Statements

  • Notices: people interacting with an AI system are told so, unless it is obvious; deployers of emotion recognition inform the people exposed to it (Article 50)
  • Explanations: what the system does, its limits, the role of human review and how to ask for a person
  • Appeal and complaint route: easy to find, with an owner and a response time
  • Incident statements: facts, impact, actions and the next update, prepared as templates with a holding statement
  • Accuracy: nothing is promised that the system cannot deliver
  • Helios: candidates are told that AI screens applications and how to reach a person (module 10)
Exam tip

Prepare the words before the incident: templates save hours and mistakes.

Running the Plan: Owners, Triggers, Channels and Rehearsal

  • Owner: one named lead, with legal, privacy and communications
  • Triggers: incidents above a set severity, regulator contact, major changes and public questions
  • Channels and timing: the right channel for each audience, within the required clocks
  • Rehearse: table-top exercises for an incident, a shutdown and a media question
  • Log what was said, to whom and when, and review after each event
  • Helios: Samira Haddad, Jonas Weber and Anika Berg form the communication group

Exam tip

A plan that is never rehearsed will fail the first time it is needed.

8IV.C.7: Put in place the policy and controls to deactivate or localize a system

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Create, so the depth is Create. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

Why Switch Off or Limit a System: The Triggers

  • Deactivate means switch the system or one feature off; localize means limit it by region, group or feature
  • Regulatory triggers: a prohibited practice in a region, a ban or an authority's order
  • Performance triggers: accuracy or fairness below thresholds, or unsafe behavior
  • Incident and rights triggers: a serious incident or a breach of people's rights
  • Supply and policy triggers: a vendor change or failure, or use outside the approved scope
  • NIST: mechanisms to supersede, disengage or deactivate systems that perform inconsistently with their intended use (MANAGE 2.4)

Exam tip

Decide the triggers before launch, not during the crisis.

Deactivation Controls: Kill Switch, Pause and Fallback

  • Feature flags: turn one feature off without stopping everything
  • Pause: stop new requests while the problem is studied
  • Kill switch: a tested way to stop the whole system at once
  • Fallback: a manual or older process so the business keeps running, with a person in the loop
  • Preserve evidence: logs, versions and data kept for investigation
  • Article 14 expects a way to intervene or stop a high-risk system

Exam tip

A kill switch that has never been tested cannot be trusted.

Localizing a System by Region, Group or Feature

  • Why localize: laws and risks differ by region, user group and feature, so one setting rarely fits all
  • Methods: regional switches (geofencing), feature flags, user-group limits and data-location settings
  • Governance: a map of each feature by region, with the legal reason and an owner
  • Helios: the hiring tool's emotion analysis is off in the EU, because the law bans inferring emotions at work (Article 5), and limited by region elsewhere until legal review
  • Test that the switch holds, so that EU applicants never reach the feature
  • Review the map when the law or the system changes

Exam tip

Localization means different settings in different places, with a record of why.

The Deactivation Policy: Authority, Steps and Records

  • Authority: who may order a shutdown, including out of hours, and who must be told
  • Criteria: clear triggers and a fast route for urgent cases
  • Steps: decide, act, verify that it worked, notify and investigate
  • Notify: users, affected people, the provider and authorities as required
  • Records: the decision, the time, the reason and who acted
  • Test it: exercises that include switching off and recovering

Exam tip

Give a named person the authority to switch off, so that nobody needs a meeting to stop a harm.

After Deactivation: Retire, Retain and Restart

  • Decide the outcome: restart after fixes, run in a limited form, or retire the system
  • Restart conditions: root cause fixed, retests passed, approvals given and communication done
  • Retire: stop access, archive the model and documents, and delete or transfer data under privacy rules and contracts (NIST names decommissioning in MANAGE 4.1)
  • Retain: logs and records for the periods that law and policy require
  • Tell people: users and partners know what ends and what replaces it
  • Learn: update the policy, the tests and the training
Exam tip

Switching off starts a process: decide whether to restart, limit or retire.

9Exam Q&A

9.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1Lucia Moreno's recruiters approve almost every candidate ranking that the Helios hiring tool produces, usually within seconds, and have never overridden one. What is the best governance response?

  • ACongratulate the team, because the high approval rate shows that the tool is accurate and that the recruiters trust it
  • BRemove the human review, because it adds no value if the reviewers agree with the tool's ranking and do not override it, and it saves time
  • CCheck whether oversight is meaningful: review samples and override rates, train recruiters, and give them time to challenge
  • DReplace the recruiters with a different group who have not yet used the tool, and then repeat the same review process
Show the answer

Answer: C. Near-total agreement and no overrides can signal automation bias. Oversight must let people understand, question and override the output, so measure it, train for it and give reviewers time to challenge.

S2A company puts a customer-facing generative AI assistant into use. Which TWO actions apply its policies to the system in use? (Select TWO.)

  • AName one business owner and set up a route for users to report problems to an owner who triages them
  • BPublish a press release and a launch blog post about the new assistant, and treat the policy work as finished
  • CWait for the first complaint from a customer before deciding who is responsible for the assistant and its answers
  • DSet rules for what users may enter, and give the documents the assistant uses owners and review dates
  • ELeave the training to the vendor, because users will learn the tool by themselves through daily use over time
Show the answer

Answer: A, D. Applying policy in use means accountable ownership, an issue route, rules for inputs and managed knowledge sources. A press release, waiting for complaints and no training do not apply any policy.

S3A company uses a vendor's language model through an interface. The vendor announces a new model version for next month. What should the company do?

  • AAccept the new version as it arrives, because vendor updates are improvements for the customers who use them
  • BRefuse updates from the vendor, so that the system stays the same after it has been launched to its users
  • CWait until users report problems, and then decide whether to test the new version or just ignore it
  • DTest the new version first using the notice terms, approve it under change control, and keep a rollback
Show the answer

Answer: D. Provider changes are changes to your system. Test the new version before it reaches users, approve it under change control and keep a rollback ready. Automatic acceptance, permanent refusal and waiting for complaints are all weak.

S4Which is the best example of a periodic check by the deployer, as distinct from continuous monitoring?

  • AAn alert that fires in the middle of the night when the error rate crosses a set threshold and pages the on-call engineer
  • BA scheduled quarterly review in which reviewers read sampled outputs, retest fairness and refresh the impact assessment
  • CA dashboard that shows live traffic to the system for the operations team throughout the working day
  • DA log entry that is written automatically each time a user submits a request to the live system
Show the answer

Answer: B. Periodic checks step back from continuous monitoring and test the system on a schedule: sample review, fairness retest and assessment refresh. Alerts, dashboards and automatic logs are continuous monitoring.

S5A deployer of a high-risk AI system keeps the automatically generated logs that are under its control. What is the best statement about how long to keep them?

  • AAt least six months, and no longer than privacy rules allow for any personal data in them
  • BTwenty-four hours, because logs are useful for fixing technical faults on the same day they are produced
  • CIndefinitely, because the logs do not contain personal data and so no time limit applies to them
  • DUntil the vendor asks for them, because the deployer has no duties about its own logs or their storage
Show the answer

Answer: A. Deployers keep the logs they control for at least six months, and logs can contain personal data, so privacy limits apply as well. Keeping them for a day, forever or only until the vendor asks is wrong.

S6A Helios recruiter pastes candidates' résumés into the customer assistant and asks it to rank them. The assistant was approved only for answering customers' questions about services. What describes this situation and the best response?

  • AA normal use, because the assistant can read the text that a user gives it, so no approval is needed
  • BDownstream harm, so Helios should wait to see whether a candidate complains about the ranking before acting
  • CAn unintended use outside the approved scope: stop it, restate the scope, add controls and assess the risk
  • DA security attack from outside the company, so the security team is the one team that needs to be told about it
Show the answer

Answer: C. The use is outside the approved scope, and it is convenient rather than malicious. Stop it, restate what the assistant is for, add access and monitoring controls, and assess the risks of using it for hiring.

S7Which TWO methods help forecast secondary or unintended uses of an AI system? (Select TWO.)

  • AAssuming that users will follow the statement of intended use, however busy they are
  • BRunning a pre-mortem that asks who else could use the system, for what, and what happens next
  • CWaiting for regulators to announce which uses of the system they consider harmful or prohibited
  • DCounting the number of pages in the user manual that explain the approved uses and the limits
  • EReviewing query logs and feedback for requests that fall outside the approved scope
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. Forecasting asks who else might use the system and checks how it is really used, through workshops, pre-mortems, red teaming and log review. Assuming compliance, waiting for regulators and counting pages do not forecast anything.

S8Samira Haddad asks for an external communication plan for the Helios assistant. Which element is most important to prepare before any incident occurs?

  • AA commitment to customers that the assistant will give correct answers under normal conditions
  • BA single technical message that is sent unchanged to customers, regulators and staff alike
  • CA rule to stay silent in public unless a journalist asks a direct question about the assistant
  • DNamed owners, triggers, channels and templates for each audience, with a rehearsal
Show the answer

Answer: D. A plan works when it has owners, triggers, channels and prepared templates for each audience, and has been rehearsed. Promising no errors, one message for everyone and silence are not plans.

S9The Helios hiring tool includes an emotion-analysis feature that is unlawful for EU applicants but may be usable elsewhere after legal review. Which control best localizes the system?

  • AA regional switch that turns the feature off for EU applicants, with a test that it holds and the reason recorded
  • BDeleting the whole hiring tool in each region where it runs, so that no feature remains in use in the company
  • CLeaving the feature on everywhere and relying on a notice that tells applicants the feature is in use, in each region
  • DAsking recruiters to ignore the emotion scores in EU cases while the feature keeps running in the background
Show the answer

Answer: A. Localizing means different settings in different places: switch the feature off in the EU, test the switch and record why. A notice does not make a prohibited use lawful, and asking recruiters to ignore scores leaves the feature running.

S10A company drafts a policy to deactivate a high-risk AI system when needed. Which TWO elements belong in it? (Select TWO.)

  • AA rule that a shutdown needs a full committee meeting, even for an urgent safety event
  • BA requirement that the kill switch be tested after the first real emergency has occurred
  • CA named authority who can order a shutdown at any hour, with clear triggers
  • DA promise that the system will never be switched off once it has been launched
  • ESteps to notify affected parties, preserve evidence and record the decision and reason
Show the answer

Answer: C, E. A deactivation policy needs a named authority with clear triggers, and steps to notify, preserve evidence and record. A committee meeting for urgent events, an untested kill switch and a promise never to switch off all defeat the purpose.

10Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Policies in use a named owner, training, issue management, data governance and a live risk register; oversight that is meaningful, not a rubber stamp
Monitoring and checks the deployer's own monitoring, change control for provider and own changes, and periodic checks that end in a decision
Records and reporting three registers, logs for at least six months, monitoring plans, and the reporting routes and clocks
Unintended use forecast with four lenses, reduce with scope, access, technical limits, monitoring and people controls
Communication audiences, notices, templates and rehearsal
Switching off triggers, kill switch and fallback, localizing by region, a policy with named authority, and restart or retire
